title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 37
paragraphs: Mardonius too, eager to begin a battle, found the sacrifices unfavorable for that purpose, though they were of good omen for him if he merely defended himself; for he too used the Greek manner of sacrifice, having as diviner Hegesistratos, an Eleian and the most famous of the Telliadai. Before these events the Spartans had captured and bound him, intending to put him to death for the much mischief they had suffered from him. In this evil state, seeing that he was running for his life and was likely to suffer much torment before death, he did a deed that is scarcely credible. Being fastened on a block bound with iron, he obtained an iron tool that had somehow been brought in, and at once devised a feat as courageous as any we know: for having first calculated how the remaining part of his foot might be freed from the block, he cut off the flat of his own foot. After that, since he was still guarded by warders, he broke through the wall and ran off to Tegea, traveling during the nights and in daytime entering a wood and resting there. Although the Lacedaemonians searched for him in full force, he reached Tegea on the third night. The Lacedaemonians were struck with great wonder both at his courage (when they saw the severed piece of foot lying there) and at their inability to find him. So he escaped them then, taking refuge at Tegea, which at that time was not friendly with the Lacedaemonians. Once healed, and having procured a wooden foot for himself, he became an open enemy of the Lacedaemonians. In the end, however, the enmity he had fallen into with the Lacedaemonians was not to his advantage; for he was caught by them while practicing divination in Zakynthos and was put to death.
